title: House of compassion
hookLine: karunaalay hain: He is the home of compassion (Jaap, harbolmana)

lines: ONE KITCHEN YOU COULD ALWAYS GO TO.
THE KETTLE WENT ON BEFORE HELLO.
cards: Some people have one kitchen like this: a grandmother's, an aunt's, a friend's mom's. You could show up unannounced, any hour, after any kind of day, and the kettle went on before you'd finished saying hello.
Nobody asked what you'd done wrong. Nobody made you earn the chair. You came in, and you were cared for, because that's what the house was for.
Some people are kind now and then. Some people are a place you can go. Jaap Sahib names the One like that second kind.

teach.h: HARBOLMANA: TWO QUICK WORDS A LINE.
teach.b: Jaap shifts into another meter, harbolmana, with tiny, fast lines of two words each, and the first is karunaalay hain. Two words fused.

Karunaa is compassion, the feeling that moves toward someone's suffering. Aalay, from aalaya, is a dwelling, a home. It hides in the name of a mountain range: Himalaya is hima, snow, plus aalaya, home.
So karunaalay is the home of compassion. You are the house where compassion lives. That's different from compassionate.

teach.h: NOT KIND SOMETIMES: A PLACE TO COME.
teach.b: A compassionate person feels it sometimes, on a good day. A home of compassion is where it lives all the time, whether anyone visits or not: the kitchen where the kettle is always ready.

Sikhs have a word close to karunaa for a human virtue: daya, kindness, mercy, often listed among the virtues a Sikh tries to grow, with truth, contentment, humility and love. And Guru Nanak gives daya a startling job.

teach.h: DAYA: THE CHILD WHO HOLDS UP THE WORLD.
teach.b: In Japji, he takes the old myth of a bull holding the earth on its back and says: the bull is dharma, righteousness, and dharma is the child of daya, of compassion. Compassion is what holds the world up.
So when Jaap calls the One the house of compassion, it also hints at what a Sikh home and a Sikh heart might try to be. Not kind sometimes. A place people can come.

how: Sikhs recite the quick harbolmana lines of Jaap Sahib each morning, and daya, compassion, is taught as one of the core virtues alongside truth, contentment, humility and love.

o: pity felt from above for those beneath you
compassion that moves toward someone's suffering
a quiet sadness felt for one's own losses

games.q: house of compassion — tap the pairs.

s: it's karunaa plus aalaya: the home where compassion lives.
in Japji, Guru Nanak calls dharma the child of compassion
the bull that holds up the earth is dharma, born of daya.
karunaalay is borrowed from the word Himalaya
they only share a part, aalaya, home: Himalaya is the home of snow, karunaalay the home of compassion.

games.q: the old myth says a bull holds the earth on its back. what does Guru Nanak say the bull really is?
games.why: in Japji, the bull is dharma, and dharma is the child of daya: compassion is what holds the world up.

practice: Think of someone who might need a place to land right now, a friend going through something, a coworker who's struggling, a lonely relative, and picture them walking into a warm kitchen while you put the kettle on.
Breathe slowly, and let the welcome be real for a moment. If you pray, you can say karunaalay hain.

wordCard.voice: Karunaa. Compassion, the feeling that moves toward suffering; and in Jaap, karunaalay, the One as the home where compassion always lives.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: karunaa, compassion; Jaap's karunaalay is its home.

carryVoice: Your line: home of compassion. Not kind sometimes: a place people can come. That's day three hundred forty-nine.
